passC.state_of_practice: Across this conference the internal game of founding is treated as a skill with mechanics, not a temperament you either have or lack. The dominant model is: conviction precedes consensus (you will toil in obscurity while people call you an idiot), self-belief arrives *after* you start rather than before, and the durable asset is your capacity to confront being wrong — Huang rebuilt NVIDIA's graphics understanding from textbooks after admitting the founding algorithm was broken, Scholl says XB-1 was over-scoped by seven years, Steinberger says he stopped making a product he loved and shipped 9,500 config options instead. Speakers converge on affect as a leading indicator rather than a byproduct: enjoyment predicts shipping velocity, and the weeks you don't enjoy show up in the diff. There is real emphasis on insulating your emotional state from external inputs that are structurally noisy — press scares, security-researcher reports produced by untested agents, Twitter dunks, the herd — because none of them track whether the work is good. What is genuinely contested is founder *formation*: whether prior institutional experience is grounding or a liability, and whether you should select your problem by what you love or by which exponential has the steepest curve and longest runway.

consensus.claim: Founders must hold conviction in a belief the market does not yet share, and expect to be dismissed for years before it becomes consensus.
consensus.evidence_quote: you need to develop conviction in a set of beliefs that nobody else um agrees with.

consensus.claim: Self-belief and competence are outputs of starting, not prerequisites — the operative trait is willingness to learn and to break the problem into survivable increments.
consensus.evidence_quote: You don't have to overcome life in one day. You just have to overcome that morning.

consensus.claim: Enjoyment of the work is load-bearing, not a luxury: it drives output quality and is the only thing that survives a decade-plus commitment.
consensus.evidence_quote: Fun is velocity. The weeks I enjoyed building, the product got visibly better.

consensus.claim: The core founder skill is confronting evidence that you were wrong and changing course, including on decisions that define the company.
consensus.evidence_quote: technology is changing all the time, and so long as you're able to confront the reality, so long as you are able to learn, the technology itself actually doesn't matter.

consensus.claim: Founders should deliberately decouple their internal state from public criticism, hype cycles, and ambient sentiment, because none of those track whether the work is working.
consensus.evidence_quote: I bet there were like a lot of days where they really felt like they got me. And like over the decade, none of them did.

consensus.claim: The prevailing founder anxiety — that AI has closed the window and the only safe move is joining a frontier lab — is unwarranted and should be actively discounted.
consensus.evidence_quote: it's hard to predict anything especially the future but I would I would take the under on this being the last couple of years to get a company going

disagreements.question: Should a founder select a problem by what they intrinsically love, or by which exponential is steepest — accepting that the work may look boring at the start?
disagreements.position_a: Select for love and enjoyment. Knowledge is changeable, passion is not; the worst outcome is being stuck for a decade in a company you don't love, and the weeks you enjoy the work are the weeks the product improves.
disagreements.position_b: Select for structural attractiveness — the exponential with the steepest curve and longest runway, or a viscerally concrete customer problem — and expect the intellectual richness to reveal itself later, even in businesses full of operational schleps.
disagreements.why_it_matters: It determines what you do when the work stops being fun — pivot toward what energizes you, or treat the dip as noise and stay on the curve. Notably Steinberger argues both sides in one talk: fun is velocity, but he would now pick something 'hard and boring' because attention, not code, is the scarce resource.

disagreements.question: Is prior experience inside an existing company an asset or a liability for a first-time founder?
disagreements.position_a: A liability, or at least heavily discounted. Expertise is steeped in the past and makes people useless at the frontier; AI fluency beats many years of domain experience, and caring — which can't be taught — should outrank credentials as a filter.
disagreements.position_b: An asset worth acquiring first. Without having worked inside a company you have no model of how companies actually build, iterate, or make decisions.
disagreements.why_it_matters: It changes whether a 21-year-old should start now or spend two years at a strong company first, and whether founders should hire young engineers into problems nobody has solved rather than credentialed veterans.

do: Before raising significant money, evaluate the success case, not just the failure case — ask whether you want to be doing this work in 10, 17, or 30 years
Be user number one, and make users two through twenty friends who will tell you the truth
Treat your own enjoyment as a shipping metric: compare what you built in weeks you enjoyed against weeks you didn't (Steinberger's joyless weeks produced config options, not features)
Redirect mental energy from 'can I do this' to 'how' — self-belief arrives late, so stop waiting for it
Run Altman's two-sided conviction test: if literally nobody shares your belief, that is evidence you may be wrong; if everybody agrees, that is also a bad sign
Optimize for the two days that matter — the worst day and the best day (Boom got to seven days of cash and a board telling Scholl to shut down)
Build a personal brand before you need it — products can be forked or cloned, a name cannot
Shrink the horizon to the next morning when the total problem is overwhelming; let the suffering come a little at a time
avoid: Drifting from building something you love into building something for everyone — Steinberger names this as the moment the project went wrong, with ~9,500 config options as the visible symptom
Letting security reporters, press scares, or hype set your emotional baseline; a correction never travels as far as a scare, and many reports are agent-generated and untested
Taking public shots at other builders — it feels like impact, compounds into nothing, and is corrosive to the person doing it
Basing business decisions on what everyone around you is saying; going with the herd ends in confusion and nowhere
Treating hard-won expertise as identity — the moment you're an expert, what you're steeped in is the past
Assuming dropping out (or any early failure) carries lasting reputational cost; as far as Collison can tell, nobody has ever cared
Waiting for the idea to become consensus before starting — successful companies are started long before their core idea is obvious

notable_outliers.claim: Being publicly ridiculed for years was net-positive for OpenAI: it deterred serious competitors and bought research time — 'only 50 people in the world believe AGI was possible, but 45 of them worked at OpenAI.'
Work-life balance is the wrong frame entirely; work-life harmony is achievable, and being a parent and a CEO are synergistic rather than competing.
A founder's personal brand is a more durable asset than any product they ship, because products can be forked or cloned and a name cannot.
Founders should reshape the organization to fit themselves rather than adopt conventional management structure — build the F1 car you personally can drive, and let the next CEO rebuild it.
Dropping out of college is reversible and reputationally free — Collison did it twice and returned in between.

passC.maturity_rationale: Six independent speakers converge tightly on the core mechanics — conviction before consensus, self-belief as an output of starting, enjoyment as a velocity signal, insulation from public noise — with no one arguing the opposite. The live edges are downstream questions of founder formation: whether to apprentice first, and whether to select a problem by love or by curve shape.
